summary: Reference for user-facing changelog craft: the public-product update feed read by end users, not the engineering changelog read by integrators.

facts.text: Reference for user-facing changelog craft: the public-product update feed read by end users, not the engineering changelog read by integrators.
Confirm the audience is the end user, not the developer/integrator.
Identify the surface. Public changelog feed / monthly digest email / in-product "What's New" panel?
Group by user benefit, not by file tree.
Lead with the outcome, not the mechanism.
Decide on visual treatment. Major UI changes get a screenshot or GIF.
Decide on version-number visibility.
Replace internal nouns with user verbs.
Quantify when honest. "3x faster" is honest if measured.
Cut entries with no user-visible effect.
Name the bug by the symptom, not the cause.
Keep one sentence per atom.
Image craft checklist:
Real product data wherever the user's eye lands.
Dark mode if your product has dark mode.
Alt text describes the change, not the chrome.
GIFs: under 5 MB, autoplay-on, loop.

facets.title: 5. Version numbers — hide, downplay, or omit

facts.text: Linear, Vercel, GitHub, Notion: no version numbers in the user changelog. The date is the version.
The version-number-only changelog. "v1.42.0 - bug fixes and improvements." This is not a changelog.
The "we're excited to announce" opener. Cut. Open with the change.
The commit-log dump. Pasting git log --oneline into a webpage.
The "improved performance" non-entry. Either quantify it or omit it.
The screenshot of nothing. Always shoot with realistic data.
The "internal upgrade" entry. "We upgraded our database to version 16." The user does not care.
Linear changelog - linear.app/changelog
Vercel changelog - vercel.com/changelog
Stripe Blog: Changelog - stripe.com/blog/changelog
Mailchimp "What's New" - mailchimp.com/whats-new
Writing the public What's New feed or changelog email that end users read, as distinct from the engineering changelog that integrators and developers read.

facts.text: Confirm the audience before drafting; a user-facing changelog and a developer or integrator changelog are different documents with different vocabulary, even for the same underlying change.

facts.text: Group entries by user benefit rather than by file tree or internal module boundaries, since the reader doesn't know or care which internal system changed.

facts.text: Replace internal nouns with user verbs, and quantify claims like “3x faster” only when the number is actually measured, not aspirational.

facts.text: A user-facing changelog necessarily loses precision that a developer changelog keeps; deciding what to cut without misleading the reader is a judgment call, not a mechanical filter.

facts.text: Dropping version numbers entirely, as Linear, Vercel, GitHub, and Notion do, works well for a continuously-deployed product but can leave integrators or support teams without a stable reference point to cite in a ticket.

facts.text: Quantified claims like “3x faster” require an actual measurement behind them; without one, honest-but-vague framing is the correct fallback, not a fabricated number.
